name: Liquidity Stress Testing
title: Liquidity Stress Testing
answer: Liquidity stress testing is the practice of projecting a firm's cash inflows and outflows under adverse scenarios to see whether it can meet obligations as they fall due. It sits inside treasury and liquidity risk management and covers contractual cash flows, behavioral assumptions, and contingent exposures. The work supports internal risk appetite, regulatory reporting, and contingency funding planning. It is distinct from capital stress testing, though the two are often run together.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Liquidity stress testing is the practice of projecting a firm's cash inflows and outflows under adverse scenarios to see whether it can meet obligations as they fall due. It sits inside treasury and liquidity risk management and covers contractual cash flows, behavioral assumptions, and contingent exposures. The work supports internal risk appetite, regulatory reporting, and contingency funding planning. It is distinct from capital stress testing, though the two are often run together.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on core banking and treasury systems, cash flow engines, balance sheet databases, and scenario libraries. Data comes from transaction systems, contractual terms, counterparty records, and market data feeds. Many firms use dedicated liquidity risk platforms or modules within asset liability management systems, with spreadsheets still common for smaller entities. AI tools can help with data mapping, anomaly detection, and scenario generation, but the calculation engine remains deterministic.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a scenario, such as a deposit run, a wholesale funding freeze, or a market shock, and maps it to cash flow assumptions. Analysts project the liquidity coverage ratio, net stable funding ratio, and survival horizon under those assumptions. They run reverse stress tests to find what would break the firm, and they document behavioral models for deposits and drawdowns. Results are challenged by risk committees and updated as conditions change.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Data provenance matters because stress results feed regulatory filings and board decisions. Firms need clear ownership of assumptions, version control, and audit trails for every scenario and override. Model risk management applies, so validation, backtesting, and documentation are expected. Regulatory expectations vary by jurisdiction, and supervisory guidance shapes much of this work. Privacy and confidentiality rules also apply to customer and counterparty data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more frequent and intraday stress testing, driven by faster payments and real time liquidity monitoring. Climate risk and nature related scenarios are being added to traditional funding shocks. AI is being used to automate data preparation, detect emerging liquidity strains, and generate plausible scenarios, though human review remains central. Firms are also linking liquidity stress results to recovery and resolution planning. The shift is from periodic exercises to continuous testing.
